claim: Extracellular recordings were made from 40 animals, 62 sensilla, and 198 odor-ORN pairs.
source: To characterize the response properties of ORNs, we made extracellular recordings from antennae of intact locusts by placing electrodes against the base of sensilla while delivering pulses of odors well-separated from each other in time (40 animals, 62 sensilla, 198 odor-ORN pairs) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of animals, sensilla, and odor-ORN pairs recorded from in the experimental methods.

claim: Sensilla contain multiple ORNs.
source: Because sensilla contain multiple ORNs (Ochieng et al., 1998), we then analyzed the recorded waveforms with a spike sorting algorithm to assign odor-elicited spikes to individual ORNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Ochieng et al., 1998.

claim: Trichoid sensilla contain 3-5 ORNs.
source: We recorded mainly from trichoid sensilla because they contain small numbers of ORNs (3–5, Ochieng et al., 1998) making spike sorting tractable
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ochieng et al., 1998.

claim: ORN responses cluster into four distinct motifs.
source: Notably, we found the responses, particularly to longer stimuli, did not fall into a continuum of patterns, but rather clustered into distinct motifs; a boot-strap analysis indicated that four motifs provided the best clustering of responses (see 'Materials and methods,' Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data analyzed using hierarchical clustering and bootstrap analysis.

claim: The four response motifs are termed excitatory, delayed, offset, and inhibitory.
source: We termed these four response motifs excitatory, delayed, offset, and inhibitory (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly names the four motifs and references figures showing them.

claim: Excitatory responses feature a sharp increase in firing rate at odor onset that decays rapidly back to baseline.
source: Excitatory responses featured a sharp increase in firing rate at the immediate onset of the odor and decayed rapidly back to baseline even as the stimulus persisted.
evidence: The manuscript provides a direct description of the excitatory motif characteristics.

claim: Delayed responses feature a slower increase in firing rate and gradual decay back to baseline.
source: Delayed responses featured a slower increase in firing rate and a gradual decay back to baseline throughout an odor pulse.
evidence: The manuscript provides a direct description of the delayed motif characteristics.

claim: Inhibitory responses feature a sharp decrease in firing rate during odor presentation that returns to baseline after odor removal.
source: Inhibitory responses featured a sharp decrease in firing rate during an odor presentation that returned to the baseline level after the odor was removed.
evidence: The manuscript provides a direct description of the inhibitory motif characteristics.

claim: Offset responses are inhibited during odor presentation but show increased firing rate exceeding baseline upon odor removal.
source: Offset responses were also inhibited during odor presentation but, upon the removal of odor, immediately showed an increase in firing rate exceeding the baseline level.
evidence: The manuscript provides a direct description of the offset motif characteristics.

claim: 1 s and 4 s odor pulses elicited similar response motifs.
source: Also, 1 s and 4 s odor pulses elicited similar results (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and references a figure showing the data.

claim: A given ORN can respond with different patterns of spiking when presented with different odors.
source: Notably, a given ORN could respond with different patterns of spiking when presented with different odors.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Response motif switching occurs with probabilities ranging from 0.31 to 0.66 for different pairs of odors.
source: This phenomenon, termed response motif switching, was not rare, occurring with probabilities ranging from 0.31 to 0.66 (mean = 0.38) for different pairs of odors (see Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific probability values derived from experimental data.

claim: Motif switching across repeated trials of the same odor is very low at 0.096.
source: By contrast, we found very little switching across repeated trials of the same odor (0.096), and an intermediate amount of switching across concentrations of the same odor (0.25, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific probability values from experimental data.

claim: Motif switching across concentrations of the same odor is 0.25.
source: By contrast, we found very little switching across repeated trials of the same odor (0.096), and an intermediate amount of switching across concentrations of the same odor (0.25, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific probability values from experimental data.

claim: Motif switching conveys information about odorant identity and concentration in a way that is robust to trial-to-trial variation.
source: Thus, motif switching appears to convey information about odorant identity and concentration in a way that is robust to trial-to-trial variation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of switching probabilities across different conditions.

claim: ORN responses adapt when odor pulses are lengthy or repeated rapidly.
source: ORN responses adapt when odor pulses are lengthy or repeated rapidly (Barrozo and Kaissling, 2002; Bau et al., 2002; Lemon and Getz, 1997; Marion-Poll and Tobin, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Each response motif shows a distinct adaptation profile.
source: Notably, each response motif showed a distinct adaptation profile (Figure 3B; see 'Materials and methods' for details of analysis).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references data in Figure 3B.

claim: The peak of excitatory motif responses decreased significantly over a train of odor pulses presented at 0.5 s inter-pulse interval.
source: The peak of excitatory motif responses decreased significantly over a train of odor pulses presented at brief, 0.5 s IPI.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistically significant changes in excitatory motif responses.

claim: The peaks of offset motif responses increased significantly with inter-pulse intervals as long as 1.0 s.
source: However, under the same stimulus conditions, the peaks of offset motif responses increased significantly, even with IPIs as long as 1.0 s; the average final response to an IPI of 0.5 s was threefold larger than the first.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistically significant increases in offset motif responses.

claim: The average final offset response to an IPI of 0.5 s was threefold larger than the first.
source: However, under the same stimulus conditions, the peaks of offset motif responses increased significantly, even with IPIs as long as 1.0 s; the average final response to an IPI of 0.5 s was threefold larger than the first.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific quantitative measurement of the increase.

claim: The delayed motif tended to increase after the first odor pulse, but this trend fell just short of statistical significance.
source: The delayed motif tended to increase after the first odor pulse, but this trend fell just short of statistical significance (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the statistical outcome for the delayed motif.

claim: The inhibitory motif appeared to show no adaptation.
source: The inhibitory motif appeared to show no adaptation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation about the inhibitory motif.

claim: The computational model was based on observations made in vivo.
source: To test this idea, we designed a computational model based on observations made in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the basis for the computational model.

claim: The model included realistic levels of input noise and variations in baseline activity.
source: The models included realistic levels of input noise and variations in baseline activity.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes features of the computational model.

claim: Model ORN responses to a single odor pulse and trains of pulses matched those found in vivo.
source: As desired, model ORN responses to a single odor pulse (Figure 4A and B) and trains of pulses (Figure 4C) matched those found in vivo (see Figures 1 and 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the model reproduced in vivo observations.

claim: The inclusion of multiple motifs adds to the complexity of ORN responses.
source: Principal component analysis of excitatory only ORN responses (blue) or all response motifs (red) shows the inclusion of multiple motifs adds to the complexity of the responses.
evidence: The claim is based on PCA analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: When only excitatory motifs were included in PCA, the first component explained nearly 30% of the variance.
source: When only excitatory motifs were included in the analysis, the first component alone explained nearly 30% of the variance and the second component added only ~1%.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative results from PCA analysis.

claim: When all motifs were included in PCA, the first component only explained ~15% of variance.
source: In contrast, when all motifs were included, the first component only explained ~15% of variance and 27 principal components were required to explain 30% of the variance (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative results from PCA analysis.

claim: 27 principal components were required to explain 30% of the variance when all motifs were included.
source: In contrast, when all motifs were included, the first component only explained ~15% of variance and 27 principal components were required to explain 30% of the variance (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative results from PCA analysis.

claim: The existence of four response motifs dramatically expanded the dimensionality of the odor representation.
source: Thus, the existence of four response motifs dramatically expanded the dimensionality of the odor representation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PCA analysis comparing excitatory-only vs. all motifs.

claim: Model versions with higher motif switching probability made it easier to distinguish two similar odors.
source: We found that the model versions that simulated higher motif switching probability made it easier to distinguish these two similar odors.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from computational modeling experiments.

claim: SVM-based classification accuracy improved as motif switching probability increased for all degrees of odor similarity.
source: When we independently varied the similarity of the odors and the probability of motif switching (see Figure 4E), support vector machine (SVM)-based classification of the ORN responses showed classification accuracy improved as motif switching probability increased for all degrees of odor similarity (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative results from SVM classification analysis.

claim: Even the lowest tested probability of motif switching (10%) substantially improved odor classification with 4 s odor pulses.
source: With 4 s odor pulses, even the lowest tested probability of motif switching (10%) substantially improved odor classification to the point that it made a difficult classification task (when test odors were very similar) as successful as an easy classification task (when odors were very different).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific results from classification analysis.

claim: Motif switching contributes substantially to successful odor classification.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that motif switching, even if infrequent, can contribute substantially to successful odor classification.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results.

claim: Long bursts within a plume led to decreased excitatory motif responses but increased delayed motif responses.
source: Notably, long bursts within a plume led to decreased excitatory motif responses but increased delayed motif responses (e.g., Figure 6A, ~9–12 s).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from plume stimulation experiments.

claim: Short bursts led to increased excitatory motif responses but did not change the delayed motif responses.
source: On the other hand, short bursts led to increased excitatory motif responses but did not change the delayed motif responses (e.g., Figure 6A, ~5 s).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from plume stimulation experiments.

claim: Filters generated from the model and from responses recorded in vivo matched closely.
source: As desired, filters generated from the model and from responses recorded in vivo matched closely (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison between model and experimental data.

claim: Different response motifs generated distinct filter waveforms.
source: We observed that different response motifs generated distinct filter waveforms, describing the different sensitivities of each motif to the temporal features of the odor plume.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from linear-nonlinear filter analysis.

claim: Filters for excitatory motifs showed that ORNs generating them were most responsive ~0.4 s after odor filaments arrived.
source: For example, filters for excitatory motifs showed that the ORNs generating them were most responsive ~0.4 s after odor filaments arrived (Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific timing information from filter analysis.

claim: ORN filters clustered by motif in PCA-reduced space.
source: We found that ORN filters clustered by motif in this space.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from PCA analysis of filters.

claim: Inhibition motifs (offset and inhibitory) and excitation motifs formed two ends of the principal filter axis.
source: Inhibition motifs (offset and inhibitory) and excitation motifs formed two ends of the principal filter axis, with the second dimension separating the delay motif from the other three (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from PCA analysis of filters.

claim: Each ORN response motif contributes uniquely to the olfactory system's representation of the odor plume's complex temporal structure.
source: This analysis revealed that each ORN response motif contributes uniquely to the olfactory system's representation of the odor plume's complex temporal structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the filter analysis results.

claim: There is a reliable relationship between the frequency of filaments within an odor plume and the distance to its source.
source: Published reports indicate a reliable relationship between the frequency of filaments within an odor plume and the distance to its source (Murlis et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Walking fruit flies navigate toward an odor source in response to both the overall frequency and inter-pulse intervals of their encounters with the odor plume.
source: Further, evidence from walking fruit flies suggests that they navigate toward an odor source in response to both the overall frequency and inter-pulse intervals of their encounters with the odor plume (Demir et al., 2020; Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018; Jayaram et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Classifiers that included the excitatory and delayed motifs were most successful in determining distance to the source.
source: We found that classifiers that included the excitatory and delayed motifs were most successful in determining distance to the source (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from classification analysis.

claim: Excitatory and delayed motif responses were less correlated with each other than the other two possible combinations.
source: Excitatory and delayed motif responses were less correlated with each other than the other two possible combinations (Figure 7D), indicating that the excitatory and delayed motif responses encoded different information about stimulus timing.
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results.

claim: The different response motifs each extract distinct information that could be used to navigate toward odor sources.
source: Together, these results show the different response motifs each extract distinct information that could be used to navigate toward odor sources.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the distance classification analysis.

source: Spiking patterns of olfactory neurons have been shown to convey information about the chemical composition of odors.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: In insects, projection neurons generate spiking patterns that change with the identity and concentration of the odor.
source: In insects, projection neurons (PNs) generate spiking patterns that change with the identity and concentration of the odor.

claim: Complex dynamics in PNs arise in part from network interactions among PNs and local inhibitory neurons within the antennal lobe driven by heterogeneities in the temporal structures of odor-elicited ORN responses.
source: These complex dynamics arise in part from network interactions among PNs and local inhibitory neurons within the antennal lobe driven by heterogeneities in the temporal structures of odor-elicited ORN responses (Martelli and Fiala, 2019; Raman et al., 2010).

claim: Kenyon cells change the timing of their spiking responses when the eliciting odor changes.
source: Deeper in the brain, Kenyon cells (KCs), driven by PNs, change the timing of their spiking responses when the eliciting odor changes (Gupta and Stopfer, 2014)

claim: Turbulent flowing media churn the headspaces above odor sources into chaotic plumes.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

source: Mice, for example, can use the separate timings of multiple odors comingled in plumes to isolate their separate sources (Ackels et al., 2021)

source: Although patterned activity originating in the olfactory environment may appear to conflict with patterned activity generated by olfactory neural circuits, combinatorial codes within the locust antennal lobes and mushroom bodies have been shown to disambiguate the two, representing not only the chemical identity and concentration of odors, but also their delivery timing (Brown et al., 2005).

claim: Even infrequent motif switching improves odor classification by increasing the distance between the spatiotemporal representations of odors.
source: Our computational model revealed that even infrequent motif switching improves odor classification by increasing the distance between the spatiotemporal representations of odors.
